results.question: What degradation problem do the authors identify when increasing the depth of plain neural networks?
results.reference_answer: As network depth increases, the accuracy of plain networks can saturate and then degrade rapidly. Importantly, the paper reports that this degradation is not caused by overfitting: deeper plain networks can have higher training error than shallower networks, indicating an optimization difficulty.

results.question: What is the main idea behind residual learning in the paper?
results.reference_answer: Instead of having stacked layers directly learn an underlying mapping H(x), the layers are trained to learn a residual mapping F(x) = H(x) - x. The original mapping is then represented as F(x) + x. The authors hypothesize that learning this residual mapping is easier to optimize.

results.question: How do shortcut connections implement the residual learning formulation?
results.reference_answer: Shortcut connections skip one or more layers and perform an identity mapping. Their outputs are added element-wise to the outputs of the stacked layers, implementing the F(x) + x formulation. Identity shortcuts add neither extra parameters nor computational complexity.

results.question: Why did the 1202-layer ResNet perform worse than the 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR-10 despite achieving very low training error?
results.reference_answer: The authors argue that the 1202-layer network was unnecessarily large for the relatively small CIFAR-10 dataset and suffered from overfitting. They note that the 1202-layer model achieved less than 0.1% training error but had a 7.93% test error, worse than the 110-layer model.
